etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English bolt, from Old English bolt, from Proto-West Germanic *bolt, from Proto-Germanic *bultaz, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeld- (“to knock, strike”). Compare Lithuanian beldu (“I knock”), baldas (“pole for striking”). Akin to Dutch and West Frisian bout, German Bolz or Bolzen, Danish bolt, Swedish bult, Icelandic bolti.

definitions.definition: A (usually) metal fastener consisting of a cylindrical body that is threaded, with a larger head on one end. It can be inserted into an unthreaded hole up to the head, with a nut then threaded on the other end; a heavy machine screw.
A sliding pin or bar in a lock or latch mechanism.

quote.citation: 1908 October, Kenneth Grahame, “Mr. Badger”, in The Wind in the Willows, New York, N.Y.: Charles Scribner’s Sons, →OCLC, page 69:
quote.text: There was the noise of a bolt shot back, and the door opened a few inches, enough to show a long snout and a pair of sleepy blinking eyes.

definitions.definition: A bar of wood or metal dropped in horizontal hooks on a door and adjoining wall or between the two sides of a double door, to prevent the door(s) from being forced open.
(military, mechanical engineering) A sliding mechanism to chamber and unchamber a cartridge in a firearm.
A small personal-armour-piercing missile for short-range use, or (in common usage though deprecated by experts) a short arrow, intended to be shot from a crossbow or a catapult.
A lightning spark, i.e., a lightning bolt.
A sudden event, action or emotion.

quote.citation: 1994, Stephen Fry, chapter 2, in The Hippopotamus:
quote.text: With a bolt of fright he remembered that there was no bathroom in the Hobhouse Room. He leapt along the corridor in a panic, stopping by the long-case clock at the end where he flattened himself against the wall.

definitions.definition: (nautical) The standard linear measurement of canvas for use at sea: 39 yards.
A large roll of fabric or similar material, as a bolt of cloth.

quote.citation: 1774 March 24, Stamford Mercury‎[1]:
quote.text: Mr. Cole, Basket-maker...has lost near 300 boults of rods

quote.citation: 1851 November 14, Herman Melville, “All Astir”, in Moby-Dick; or, The Whale, 1st American edition, New York, N.Y.: Harper & Brothers; London: Richard Bentley, →OCLC, page 106:
quote.text: Not only were the old sails being mended, but new sails were coming on board, and bolts of canvas, and coils of rigging; in short, everything betokened that the ship's preparations were hurrying to a close.

definitions.definition: A sudden spring or start; a sudden leap aside.
A sudden flight, as to escape creditors.

quote.citation: 1887, Charles Reade, Compton Reade, Charles Reade, Dramatist, Novelist, Journalist: A Memoir:
quote.text: This gentleman was so hopelessly involved that he contemplated a bolt to America — or anywhere.

definitions.definition: (US, politics) A refusal to support a nomination made by the party with which one has been connected; a breaking away from one's party.
An iron to fasten the legs of a prisoner; a shackle; a fetter.

definitions.definition: A burst of speed or efficiency.

quote.citation: 2018 June 17, Barney Ronay, “Mexico’s Hirving Lozano stuns world champions Germany for brilliant win”, in Katharine Viner, editor, The Guardian‎[2], London: Guardian News & Media, →ISSN, →OCLC, archived from the original on 5 August 2019:

definitions.definition: A stalk or scape (of garlic, onion, etc).

quote.text: All kinds of vegetables may be used as a topping, but the best are strongly flavoured ones without too much moisture, such as celery, garlic bolts, chives, scallions, or various beans (long beans, green beans etc.) ...

quote.text: She ordered Cat's Ear Noodles heaped with garlic bolts and tomatoes, the broth thick with cumin, laced with black vinegar. The girl caught her accent, the sibilant sing-song of the south, and smiled, tilting her head questioningly.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To connect or assemble pieces using a bolt.
(transitive, figurative) To affix in a crude or unnatural manner.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To secure a door by locking or barring it.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To flee, to depart, to accelerate away suddenly.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To escape.
(transitive) To cause to start or spring forth; to dislodge (an animal being hunted).

definitions.definition: (intransitive, botany, of lettuce, spinach, garlic, onion, etc) To produce flower stalks and flowers or seeds quickly or prematurely; to form a bolt (stalk or scape); to go to seed.

quote.text: Though amid all the smoking horror and diabolism of a sea-fight, sharks will be seen longingly gazing up to the ship’s decks, like hungry dogs round a table where red meat is being carved, ready to bolt down every killed man that is tossed to them;

definitions.definition: (transitive) To drink one's drink very quickly; to down a drink.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English bulten, from Anglo-Norman buleter, Old French bulter (modern French bluter), from a Germanic source originally meaning "bag, pouch" cognate with Middle High German biuteln (“to sift”), from Proto-Germanic *buzdô (“beetle, grub, swelling”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰūs- (“to move quickly”). Cognate with Dutch buidel.

definitions.definition: To sift, especially through a cloth.
To sift the bran and germ from wheat flour.
To separate, assort, refine, or purify by other means.
